pos: n. phr. (the great wonder of Revelation 12, the woman who brings forth the man child)
etymology: Greek gynē peribeblēmenē ton hēlion — periballō, to throw around, hence clothed or arrayed; the sun, moon and twelve stars together recall Joseph's dream of the sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowing to him.
biblical_def: “And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars: And she being with child cried, travailing in birth.” She brings forth a man child who is to rule all nations and who is caught up unto God and to His throne; the dragon stands by to devour the child, fails, pursues the woman into a wilderness where she is nourished, and at last makes war with the remnant of her seed, which keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus Christ. The imagery identifies her. The crown of twelve stars and the sun and moon are Joseph's dream, which is to say the covenant people; the man child who rules all nations is Christ; and the remnant of her seed at the chapter's end is the church under persecution. The woman is therefore the covenant community of God — Israel out of whom Christ came, continuing as the church He purchased — and the chapter's comfort is that the dragon fails at the cradle, fails in heaven, fails in the wilderness, and is reduced to making war on her children with a short time remaining. The Reformed have read her this way since the Reformation, and the structure of the chapter requires it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Clothe, to put garments on; to cover with raiment. Wonder, that emotion which is excited by novelty, or by something strange or great; a prodigy. A woman clothed with the sun, Revelation 12:1, the covenant people out of whom Christ came.
webster_full: Clothe, to put garments on; to cover with or as with raiment.
Wonder, a strange or marvellous thing; a prodigy or portent.
Greek sēmeion, a sign; the AV renders it ‘wonder’ here.
Greek periballō, to throw around; hence arrayed or clothed with.
The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph's dream, Genesis 37:9.
scriptures: Rev 12:1
And there appeared a great wonder in heaven; a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars:
Rev 12:2
And she being with child cried, travailing in birth, and pained to be delivered.
Rev 12:5
And she brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron: and her child was caught up unto God, and to his throne.
And the dragon was wroth with the woman, and went to make war with the remnant of her seed, which keep the commandments of God, and have the testimony of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Rome identifies the woman as Mary and builds Marian dogma on the figure; others make her a purely future national Israel detached from the church that the chapter itself names as her seed.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman Catholic exposition reads the woman as the virgin Mary and has used the verse in support of her queenship and bodily assumption, with the crown of twelve stars taken as her diadem. The chapter will not carry it. The woman flees into a wilderness and is nourished there for a prophetic period, is pursued by a flood from the dragon's mouth, and has a remnant of her seed who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus — none of which is the history of Mary and all of which is the history of the covenant people under persecution. The Marian reading also feeds a devotion Scripture nowhere commands; the New Testament honours Mary as blessed among women and directs worship to her Son alone.

The dispensational reading errs in the opposite direction, assigning the woman exclusively to a national Israel of a future tribulation and severing her from the church, though the chapter's own last verse makes the persecuted remnant of her seed those who have the testimony of Jesus Christ — which is the church. The principle to recover is the continuity of the one covenant people. Christ came out of Israel; the church is the Israel of God into which believing Gentiles are grafted; and the dragon's war against the woman's seed is the persecution the saints have borne in every age, overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.
roots_summary: Greek sēmeion, a sign (AV ‘wonder’); periballō, to array or clothe — the sun, moon and twelve stars are Joseph's dream, the covenant people.
roots_lines: Greek gynē, a woman; here a sign appearing in heaven.
Greek sēmeion, a sign or portent; rendered ‘wonder’ in the AV.
Greek periballō, to throw around, hence clothed or arrayed with.
The twelve stars answer the twelve tribes; compare Genesis 37:9.
Her remnant seed keep God's commandments and the testimony of Jesus, Revelation 12:17.
usage: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet
upon her head a crown of twelve stars
the remnant of her seed, which keep the commandments of God

pos: n. phr. (the conflict of Michael and his angels with the dragon, and the dragon's casting out)
etymology: Greek polemos en tōiouranōi — polemos, war or battle, not a skirmish; ouranos, heaven; the outcome is given by eblthē, he was cast out, a passive naming God as the one who casts.
biblical_def: “And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels, And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven.” The chapter then names the loser plainly — that great dragon, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world — and the heaven rejoices with a loud voice that the accuser of the brethren is cast down, overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of the saints' testimony. Three points govern the doctrine. First, the war is real but it is not even: the dragon fights and prevailed not, and the verb of his casting out is passive, which is to say God did the casting. Second, the ground of the victory named in the eleventh verse is not angelic strength but the blood of the Lamb, so the decisive event is Calvary. Third, the dragon's response is war on earth against the woman's seed, with great wrath because he knoweth that he hath but a short time — the persecution of the church is thus the rage of a defeated enemy, not the advance of a winning one. Reformed expositors have connected this casting out with Christ's own words that He beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven and that now is the prince of this world judged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): War, a contest between nations or states carried on by force. Heaven, the region above; the dwelling of God and His holy angels. War in heaven, Revelation 12:7, the casting out of the dragon by Michael and his angels.
webster_full: War, a contest or conflict carried on by force between opposing parties.
Heaven, the region above the earth; the dwelling place of God and His angels.
Greek polemos, a war or battle, a sustained conflict rather than a skirmish.
Greek ischyō ouk, prevailed not — of the dragon and his angels.
Overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, Revelation 12:11.
scriptures: Rev 12:7
And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon; and the dragon fought and his angels,
Rev 12:8
And prevailed not; neither was their place found any more in heaven.
Rev 12:9
And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: The passage is turned into a cosmic dualism of two comparable powers, or else mined for a technique of spiritual combat that displaces the blood of the Lamb named as the ground of victory.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular treatments make this a battle between near-equals whose outcome hung in doubt, which is dualism and not Christianity. Scripture's dragon is a creature; he fights and prevails not; the verb of his expulsion is passive, which means God cast him out; and he operates throughout the book within limits set for him, down to the short time he is allowed. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds here as everywhere: Satan is real, powerful, and wholly under God's government, so that even his rage serves the purposes of the One who permits it.

The second error belongs to the spiritual-warfare industry, which reads the chapter as a manual — territorial spirits to be bound, strongholds to be named, formulas to be pronounced — and leaves out the eleventh verse, where the saints overcome by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony and by not loving their lives unto the death. Those are the given weapons: the atonement, confession of the truth, and willingness to die. The principle to recover is that the Christian's part in this war is faith, witness and endurance, armed with the whole armour of God which is doctrine and prayer, and that the decisive battle was fought at the cross and is not being refought now.
roots_summary: Greek polemos, war; ischyō ouk, prevailed not; the passive ‘was cast out’ names God as the agent — and Revelation 12:11 names the blood of the Lamb as the victory.
roots_lines: Greek polemos, war or battle; a sustained conflict, not a skirmish.
Greek drakōn, the dragon, named as the Devil and Satan in Revelation 12:9.
Greek ischyō, to prevail or be strong — here denied to the dragon.
Greek ekballō in the passive, was cast out; God is the unnamed agent.
Compare Satan falling as lightning from heaven, Luke 10:18.
usage: And there was war in heaven
Michael and his angels fought against the dragon
they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb

pos: n. phr. (the martyrs seen at the opening of the fifth seal, crying How long)
etymology: Greek hypokatō tou thysiastēriou tas psychas — hypokatō, underneath; thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice; the place is significant, for the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar.
biblical_def: “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” They are given white robes and told to rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants should be killed as they were. The location carries the doctrine: the blood of the sacrifices was poured at the foot of the altar, and these are souls whose lives were poured out as an offering, which is exactly how Paul speaks of his own death. Several things follow. The martyrs are conscious, vocal, and in heaven immediately after death, which settles the intermediate state. Their prayer is for judgment and vengeance, and it is not rebuked but answered with a white robe and a timetable — so the imprecations of the Psalter are not a lower morality the New Testament outgrew. And the answer given is that a number must yet be filled, which means the church's suffering is measured and counted by God. Nothing here suggests the martyrs are to be prayed to; they are the ones praying.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Altar, an elevated place on which sacrifices were offered. Soul, the spiritual, immortal part of man. I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain, Revelation 6:9, the martyrs at the opening of the fifth seal.
webster_full: Altar, an elevated place or structure on which sacrifices were offered to God.
Soul, the spiritual and immortal part of man, distinct from the body.
Greek thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice, at whose base blood was poured.
Greek psychē, the soul; here conscious, vocal, and in heaven.
They are told to rest yet for a little season, Revelation 6:11.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
Rev 6:11

And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled.
Rev 20:4

And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.
corruption_summary: The passage is pressed into the invocation of saints and the cult of relics beneath altars, and from the other side emptied by soul-sleep, which cannot account for souls that speak.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's practice of placing relics beneath altars and of invoking the martyrs as intercessors has long appealed to this verse. The text gives no warrant for either. These souls pray to God, not to the living, and no one in the chapter prays to them; their cry is a plea for divine judgment, and the answer comes from God alone. Scripture directs prayer to God through the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the New Testament's only priesthood besides His is that of all believers. A doctrine of saintly mediation built on a verse in which the saints themselves are petitioners inverts the passage.

The denial of the conscious intermediate state must handle the verse no better. Souls that cry with a loud voice, are addressed, are given robes, and are told to wait a little season are not asleep or non-existent. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed confessions state: the souls of the righteous, being made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies. And with it recover the martyrs' prayer itself, which the church has grown shy of — How long, O Lord, holy and true — a petition for justice that God answers and does not reprove.
roots_summary: Greek thysiastērion, the altar at whose base sacrificial blood was poured; psychē, soul — lives poured out as an offering, conscious and crying for judgment.
roots_lines: Greek thysiastērion, the altar of sacrifice; blood was poured at its base.
Greek psychē, the soul, here conscious, vocal, and clothed in white.
Greek sphazō, to slay or slaughter, used of a sacrificial killing.
Greek heōs pote, how long — the martyrs' cry, Revelation 6:10.
Compare Paul poured out as an offering, 2 Timothy 4:6, and Philippians 2:17.
usage: I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain
How long, O Lord, holy and true
that they should rest yet for a little season

word: Keys of Hell and of Death
pronunciation: KEEZ uv HEL and uv DETH
pos: n. phr. (Christ's claim to hold the authority over the grave and the unseen world)
etymology: Greek tas kleis tou hadou kai tou thanatou — kleis, a key, the standing figure of authority to open and shut; hadēs, the unseen world of the dead, rendered hell here by the AV; thanatos, death.
biblical_def: The risen Christ says to John, “I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.” John had fallen at His feet as dead and is told, Fear not. The claim is precisely ordered: first the resurrection as an accomplished fact, then the endless life that follows it, then the keys as the consequence of both. A key in Scripture is authority to open and to shut — the key of the house of David, the keys of the kingdom — and these particular keys govern the grave and the realm of the dead. The One who holds them entered that realm Himself and came out, which is what qualifies Him to hold them. Two comforts follow and the chapter draws the first of them explicitly: John need not be afraid, and neither need any believer, since no man dies except by the opening of a door Christ holds, and none stays shut in behind it. The apostle says Christ took part of flesh and blood that through death He might destroy him that had the power of death, and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. Death remains an enemy, but it is a defeated enemy with its keys on another's belt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Key, an instrument for shutting or opening a lock; figuratively, that which opens or explains. Hell, the place of the dead; the place of punishment for the wicked. The keys of hell and of death, Revelation 1:18, Christ's authority over the grave.
webster_full: Key, an instrument for opening or shutting a lock; hence, authority to admit.
Hell, in the AV, the unseen place of the dead; also the place of punishment.
Greek kleis, a key; the figure of authority to open and to shut.
Greek hadēs, the unseen world of the dead, rendered ‘hell’ here.
Spoken by the risen Christ with ‘Fear not’, Revelation 1:17-18.
scriptures: Rev 1:18
I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death.
Rev 1:17
And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last:
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
corruption_summary: The keys are claimed for the papacy by conflation with Matthew 16, and in some teaching are handed to the believer as an authority over death the verse reserves to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's doctrine of the papal keys rests on Matthew 16:19 and the keys of the kingdom of heaven; it is a separate text with a separate object, and it does not reach these keys at all. The keys of hell and of death are claimed by Christ in the first person, and the ground He gives is His own dying and rising — I am he that liveth, and was dead. No man can hold them on that basis, and no office can inherit them. The Reformed answer to the keys of Matthew 16 is that the authority given was to the apostles and through them to the church in the ministry of the word and discipline; the keys of Revelation 1 were never given to anyone, because the One holding them does not retire.

A different overreach appears where believers are taught to exercise authority over death itself, commanding sickness and the grave as though the keys had been delegated. Scripture keeps them where this verse puts them. The last enemy to be destroyed is death, and it will be destroyed by Christ at His coming; until then saints die, and die in faith, and their dying is precious in the LORD's sight. The principle to recover is the pastoral force of the Fear not that introduces the claim: a Christian facing death looks not to his own authority but to the hands that hold the keys, pierced and alive for evermore.
roots_summary: Greek kleis, a key — authority to open and shut; hadēs, the unseen realm of the dead; thanatos, death — held by the One who died and lives for evermore.
roots_lines: Greek kleis, a key; in Scripture the figure of authority to open and shut.
Greek hadēs, the unseen world of the dead, the AV's ‘hell’ here.
Greek thanatos, death, named as the last enemy to be destroyed.
Grounded in ‘I am he that liveth, and was dead’, Revelation 1:18.
Compare the key of the house of David, Isaiah 22:22, Revelation 3:7.
usage: I am he that liveth, and was dead
and have the keys of hell and of death
Fear not; I am the first and the last

pos: n. phr. (the sound of God's voice and of the redeemed multitude, likened to great waters)
etymology: Greek phōnē hydatōn pollōn — phōnē, a voice or sound; hydata polla, many waters; the figure renders Ezekiel's qol mayim rabbim, used there of the voice of the God of Israel.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs at three heights in Revelation and once in Ezekiel, and the pattern is instructive. Ezekiel hears the voice of the God of Israel, and His voice was like a noise of many waters. John hears Christ's voice in the first chapter as the voice of many waters. Then the same comparison is used twice of the redeemed: a voice from heaven as the voice of many waters, which is the harpers harping with their harps and the hundred forty and four thousand singing a new song; and at the marriage of the Lamb, a voice as of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia. The figure means volume and depth — not a trickle but a cataract, the sound of a river in flood or surf on a shore, a sound that cannot be talked over. That the same comparison is used of God's own voice and of His people's praise is the point worth preaching. The praise of the redeemed is made to answer the voice of God in kind, and the congregation whose singing is thin has something to aspire to. Scripture's heaven is loud, and its loudness is all vocal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Voice, sound uttered by the mouth; any sound made by percussion or motion. Waters, the collection or flood of water. The voice of many waters, Revelation 14:2, the sound of God's voice and of the praise of the redeemed.
webster_full: Voice, sound uttered by the mouth; also any sound of motion or percussion.
Waters, a collection or flood of water, as a river or the sea.
Greek phōnē, a voice, sound, or utterance.
Greek hydata polla, many waters — volume and depth, not a trickle.
Renders Ezekiel's qol mayim rabbim, of the voice of the God of Israel.
scriptures: Rev 14:2
And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps:
Rev 19:6
And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
Rev 1:15
And his feet like unto fine brass, as if they burned in a furnace; and his voice as the sound of many waters.
Eze 43:2
And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east: and his voice was like a noise of many waters: and the earth shined with his glory.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; its neglect shows rather in congregational worship that has made the people's voice the quietest thing in the room.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No rival doctrine attaches to the phrase, and it carries no contested history. Where it is lost is in practice. Revelation likens the praise of the redeemed to the sound of a flood and to mighty thunderings, and Scripture's commands to sing are addressed to the whole assembly, speaking to themselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. A service in which amplified performers are loud and the congregation is barely audible has reversed the picture, whatever its style.

The principle to recover follows from the figure's double use. The same comparison is made of God's own voice in Ezekiel and of His people's praise in Revelation, which sets the standard high and locates it in the people rather than in the instruments — the heavenly sound John hears is harpers and singers, and the words are intelligible, a new song and an Alleluia. Congregational singing of substantial words by the whole gathered church is therefore not a matter of taste but the earthly form of the sound Revelation describes, and the regulative principle keeps it where Scripture puts it: the people's own voices, singing truth.
roots_summary: Greek phōnē hydatōn pollōn, voice of many waters — used of the voice of the God of Israel in Ezekiel, of Christ's voice, and of the praise of the redeemed.
roots_lines: Greek phōnē, a voice or sound, whether of speech or of nature.
Greek hydata polla, many waters; the figure is volume, depth and force.
Used of Christ's own voice in the vision, Revelation 1:15.
Used of the redeemed singing a new song with harps, Revelation 14:2.
Renders Ezekiel's qol mayim rabbim of God's voice, Ezekiel 43:2.
usage: as the voice of many waters
and as the voice of a great thunder
as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia

pos: n. phr. (the scars of persecution Paul bore in his body, his answer to the circumcision party)
etymology: Greek ta stigmata tou kūriou Iēsou — stigma, a brand or mark pricked into the flesh, used of the marks branded on a slave to show whose he was; the plural gives the English word stigmata.
biblical_def: Galatians closes in Paul's own hand and ends with this: “From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.” The letter has been a sustained battle against men who were compelling Gentile believers to be circumcised so that they might glory in their flesh. Paul answers with marks of his own. The word is stigmata, the brand burned or pricked into a slave to show whose property he was, and his are the scars of the work — thrice beaten with rods, five times scourged, once stoned and left for dead, as he recounts to the Corinthians. His argument is therefore not a claim to superior spiritual experience but an appeal to ownership. These men boast in a mark made by a knife in a ceremony; Paul carries the brand of his Master got in His service, and that settles who he belongs to. The two verses before it set the terms: God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. The marks are not the ground of his boasting; the cross is, and the marks are simply the evidence of a servant who has been where his Master sent him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Mark, a visible line, impression or trace; a character or stamp impressed. Brand, a mark made by burning with a hot iron. I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus, Galatians 6:17, the scars of persecution borne as a slave's brand.
webster_full: Mark, a visible impression, line, or trace made upon a thing.
Brand, a mark made by burning with a hot iron, as upon a slave or beast.
Greek stigma (plural stigmata), a mark pricked or branded into the flesh.
Used of the brand identifying a slave's owner in the ancient world.
Set against those who would glory in the flesh, Galatians 6:13.
scriptures: Gal 6:17
From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.
Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;
Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body.
corruption_summary: The phrase was taken over to name the miraculous reproduction of Christ's wounds in medieval mystics, a sense wholly absent from Paul, whose marks were the scars of beatings.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval and modern phenomenon called stigmata — the appearance of Christ's five wounds in the body of a mystic, reported of Francis of Assisi and others since — borrows its name from this verse and has nothing of its meaning. Paul's marks are enumerated elsewhere in his own hand and they are a catalogue of violence done to him by men: rods, scourges, stones, shipwreck, a night and a day in the deep. Nothing in Galatians suggests a miracle, and nothing in the New Testament commends the pursuit of visible wound-marks as a sign of nearness to Christ. Private revelations and bodily prodigies are not canonical evidence, whatever the sincerity of those who report them, and a devotion built on them has moved the ground of assurance from the cross to the believer's body.

A second and milder misuse turns the phrase into a boast of hardship generally, so that any wearying of ministry becomes a mark of the Lord Jesus. Paul's context is persecution for the gospel he had just defended, in a letter that refuses to glory in anything but the cross. The principle to recover is the slave-brand sense of the word. A servant's scars prove ownership, not merit; they close an argument about whose he is, and they are worn without self-pity by a man whose only boasting is in Christ crucified.
roots_summary: Greek stigma, a brand pricked into a slave's flesh to mark his owner — Paul's scars of scourging and stoning, set against the circumcision party's glorying in the flesh.
roots_lines: Greek stigma (plural stigmata), a mark pricked or branded into the flesh.
Used of the brand identifying the owner of a slave or of cattle.
Greek bastazō, to bear or carry — ‘I bear in my body’.
Paul's own catalogue of the scars, 2 Corinthians 11:24-25.
Preceded by glorying in nothing save the cross, Galatians 6:14.
usage: I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus
From henceforth let no man trouble me

pos: n. phr. (the Lord's word to Ananias concerning Saul of Tarsus)
etymology: Greek skeuos eklogēs — literally a vessel of choosing or of election; skeuos, an implement or article made for a use, and eklogē, the noun of election, the same word used of God's electing purpose in Romans.
biblical_def: Ananias objects, reasonably, that the man he is being sent to has done much evil to the saints and holds authority to bind believers in Damascus. “But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake.” The Greek is a Hebraism — a vessel of election — and the figure is the potter's, running through Scripture from Jeremiah's workshop to the vessels of mercy in Romans and the vessels unto honour of the second letter to Timothy. Three things are stated and each belongs to the doctrine of election. The choosing is the Lord's and it is prior: Saul is a chosen vessel while he is still the church's persecutor, breathing out threatenings. The purpose is named: to bear a name, before Gentiles, kings and Israel, which is service and not status. And the cost is announced in the same breath: how great things he must suffer. Election in Scripture is never a bare privilege; it is a choosing to a work, and in this case the work was chains. Paul afterwards wrote that he laboured more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Chosen, selected from a number; elected; appointed. Vessel, a utensil; in Scripture, a person considered as an instrument of God's designs. He is a chosen vessel unto me, Acts 9:15, the Lord's word to Ananias about Saul.
webster_full: Chosen, selected from a number; elected; appointed to a purpose.
Vessel, a utensil or instrument; in Scripture, a person used of God.
Greek skeuos, a vessel, implement, or article prepared for a use.
Greek eklogē, election or choosing; literally ‘a vessel of election’.
The choosing is joined to suffering in the next verse, Acts 9:16.
scriptures: Act 9:15
But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:
Act 9:16
For I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake.
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
corruption_summary: The phrase is turned into a title of personal destiny and anointing, detached both from the sovereign choosing that grants it and from the suffering named in the next verse.
corruption_paragraphs: In much popular preaching “a chosen vessel” has become a compliment a man accepts about himself — a word over a life, a sign of special anointing — and the two halves of the Lord's sentence that would correct it are left unquoted. The first is the choosing: Saul is a chosen vessel unto me, and he is so while still a persecutor, which means the choosing explains nothing about him and everything about God. The second is the next verse: I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake. A doctrine of chosenness that promises platform and omits chains is not this text.

The arminian reading errs differently, making the choosing a response to something God foresaw in Saul. Luke's narrative leaves no room: the man was breathing out threatenings and slaughter and was struck down on the road. Paul's own account of it says God separated him from his mother's womb and called him by His grace. The principle to recover is the one the apostle himself drew — by the grace of God I am what I am — and with it the purpose clause, for the vessel is chosen to bear a name before Gentiles, kings and Israel. Election is to service, and the measure of it is faithfulness in that service, not the sense of being singled out.
roots_summary: Greek skeuos eklogēs, a vessel of election — the potter's figure joined to the noun of election, with the purpose and the suffering both named by the Lord.
roots_lines: Greek skeuos, a vessel or implement made and kept for a use.
Greek eklogē, election or choosing — literally a vessel of election.
A Hebraism: the genitive of quality, hence ‘a chosen vessel’.
Purpose named: to bear His name before Gentiles, kings and Israel.
Cost named in the next verse: how great things he must suffer, Acts 9:16.
usage: he is a chosen vessel unto me
to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel
I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake

pos: n. phr. (the reward laid up for Paul and for all that love Christ's appearing)
etymology: Greek ho tēs dikaiosynēs stephanos — stephanos, the victor's or festal wreath rather than a king's diadem; with dikaiosynē, righteousness; the genitive names what the crown consists of or answers to.
biblical_def: Writing near his death, Paul says, “Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.” The word is stephanos, the wreath given to a victor at the games or worn at a feast, not the diadem of a monarch, and Paul has just used the athletic figure — I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course. Four things are exact. The crown is laid up, already reserved and not yet worn. It is given by the Lord as the righteous judge, so it is no arbitrary favour but a just award to a work He Himself wrought in His servant. It is given at that day, which the chapter identifies as His appearing, so it is not received at death but at the last. And it is emphatically not for apostles only, but for all that love His appearing — a mark that belongs to every true believer and not to a class of heroes. The dictionary's entries on the crown of life and the crown of glory treat the two companion wreaths; all three are given, none earned, and each is cast before the throne by those who wear it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Crown, an ornament worn on the head by kings; a garland; a reward of victory. Righteousness, purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity to the divine law. A crown of righteousness, 2 Timothy 4:8, the reward laid up for all that love Christ's appearing.
webster_full: Crown, an ornament for the head; a garland; the reward of a victor.
Righteousness, conformity of heart and life to the divine law.
Greek stephanos, a victor's or festal wreath, not a royal diadem.
Greek apokeimai, to be laid up or reserved — already kept in store.
Given at His appearing to all that love it, 2 Timothy 4:8.
scriptures: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
Jas 1:12
Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.
corruption_summary: The crown is made a wage earned by achievement, which turns reward into merit; or it is denied altogether, as though any talk of reward compromised grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as wages, the verse feeds a doctrine of merit the whole letter denies. Paul has written in the same letter that God saved us and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace; and the crown is said to be given by the righteous judge, which is the language of an award and not of a debt. Rome's treasury of merit and every scheme of works-righteousness founders here, because what the judge is rewarding is the fruit of grace He Himself supplied. Augustine's words have been the Reformed answer for centuries: when God crowns our merits He crowns His own gifts.

The opposite reaction, common among those anxious to guard grace, refuses to speak of reward at all and so loses a strong New Testament motive. Scripture holds out the crown without embarrassment, tells us to lay up treasure in heaven, and says Moses had respect unto the recompence of the reward. The principle to recover is the balance the text itself keeps. The crown is laid up by grace, awarded justly for what grace produced, and given to all that love His appearing — a love which is itself the Spirit's work, and which is the one qualification the verse names.
roots_summary: Greek stephanos, a victor's wreath, not a diadem; apokeimai, laid up in store; given by the righteous judge at His appearing, and to all who love it.
roots_lines: Greek stephanos, the wreath of a victor or feast-guest, not a king's diadem.
Greek dikaiosynē, righteousness; the genitive of what the crown answers to.
Greek apokeimai, to be laid up or reserved, already in store.
Greek ho dikaios kritēs, the righteous judge, who gives it.
Companions: the crown of life, James 1:12, and of glory, 1 Peter 5:4.

which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day

pos: n. phr. (third of the three graces Paul remembered in the Thessalonians)
etymology: Greek hē hypomonē tēs elpidos — hypomonē, endurance, literally a remaining-under a weight, stronger than mere forbearance; elpis, hope, confident expectation; the genitive names hope as the spring of the endurance.
biblical_def: “Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father.” Paul remembers three things in this young church, and each is a grace joined to its proper effect: faith works, love labours, and hope endures. Hypomonē is not passivity. It is the word for remaining under a load without giving way — the soldier who holds his ground, the beast that does not shift its burden — and the New Testament uses it of the believer's continuance under affliction. What Paul credits here is that the Thessalonians' endurance has a cause outside itself: it is the patience of hope, and the hope is in our Lord Jesus Christ, which this letter spells out as waiting for God's Son from heaven. That is the Reformed account of Christian perseverance. A man endures because he expects something certain, and the certainty is a Person and His appearing, not an improvement in circumstances. Paul says as much elsewhere: if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it. Where hope is vague the endurance fails; where hope is definite the endurance holds, and it holds, as this verse says, in the sight of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Patience, the suffering of afflictions with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring. Hope, a desire of some good, accompanied with expectation of obtaining it. Patience of hope, 1 Thessalonians 1:3, the endurance that springs from a definite expectation of Christ.
webster_full: Patience, the bearing of afflictions calmly; endurance without murmuring.
Hope, desire of good with expectation of obtaining it; confident expectation.
Greek hypomonē, endurance; literally a remaining-under a weight.
Greek elpis, hope; confident expectation, not wishful uncertainty.
Third of the triad with work of faith and labour of love, 1 Thessalonians 1:3.
scriptures: Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father;
Rom 8:25
But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
Heb 6:19
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
corruption_summary: Hope is weakened into wishing and patience into mere temperament, so that the New Testament's strongest word for endurance under a load is read as a pleasant disposition.
corruption_paragraphs: Ordinary English has worn hope down to a wish — one hopes it will not rain — and once that sense is carried into the verse the patience it produces becomes a vague cheerfulness. The New Testament's elpis is confident expectation of a promised thing, called in Hebrews an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and in Titus the blessed hope and glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. Endurance drawn from an anchor is a different thing from endurance drawn from optimism, and only the first survives the kind of affliction this letter was written into.

The companion error treats patience as a native temperament — some people are patient — when hypomonē is a word for holding a position under weight and is everywhere in the New Testament the fruit of something else: tribulation worketh patience, the trying of your faith worketh patience, and here hope works it. The principle to recover is the chain Paul and James both give. Affliction is the occasion, hope in the returning Christ is the spring, and endurance is the result, wrought by the Spirit and not by disposition — which is why a weak believer may have it and a strong temperament may not.
roots_summary: Greek hypomonē, a remaining-under a load; elpis, confident expectation — the genitive names hope as the spring, and the hope is in the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
roots_lines: Greek hypomonē, endurance; from hypo, under, and menō, to remain.
Greek elpis, hope; confident expectation of a promised good.
Paired with ergon pisteos, work of faith, and kopos agapēs, labour of love.
Hope's object named in the same letter: God's Son from heaven, 1 Thessalonians 1:10.
Called an anchor of the soul, sure and steadfast, Hebrews 6:19.
usage: and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ
your work of faith, and labour of love
in the sight of God and our Father

pos: n. phr. (a divine title, spoken by Samuel to Saul concerning God's unchangeableness)
etymology: Hebrew netsach Yisrael — netsach, which the AV margin itself glosses “or, Eternity, or, Victory”; the root carries endurance, perpetuity and the pre-eminence of one who outlasts and overcomes, so the title names God as Israel's unfailing permanence.
biblical_def: Saul has spared Agag and the best of the spoil, offered sacrifice as his excuse, and been told that to obey is better than sacrifice. When he clutches at Samuel's mantle and tears it, Samuel gives him the reason the kingdom will not be restored: “And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.” The title is rare and weighty. The Hebrew word is netsach, which the translators' own margin glosses as Eternity and as Victory, and either reading serves: God is Israel's permanence and Israel's triumph, the one who does not fail or change. The context is what makes the title a judgment. Saul wants the sentence reconsidered, and the answer is that the One who passed it is not a man that He should change His mind. The same chapter says two verses earlier that it repented the LORD that He had set up Saul, which teaches the reader how such language works: Scripture speaks of God relenting in the language of His dealings with men, and in the same breath denies that He is mutable in His nature or His purpose. The Reformed doctrine of divine immutability stands exactly here, and so does the sinner's only ground of hope, since an unchangeable God is as unchangeable in His promises as in His threatenings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Strength, that property of a body by which it sustains the application of force without breaking; firmness; power. Israel, the covenant name given to Jacob and to the nation from him. The Strength of Israel, 1 Samuel 15:29, a divine title naming God's unchangeableness.
webster_full: Strength, that property by which a body sustains force without breaking; firmness.
Israel, the name given to Jacob and to the nation descended from him.
Hebrew netsach, perpetuity, endurance; the AV margin adds ‘Eternity’ and ‘Victory’.
Hebrew shaqar, to lie or deal falsely — denied of Him in the same verse.
Hebrew nacham, to repent or relent — ‘he is not a man, that he should repent’.
scriptures: And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
corruption_summary: Open theism and process theology deny the very attribute this title names, and the verse is also pressed flat in the other direction until God's relenting language in the same chapter is treated as a mere figure of nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: Open theism, in Pinnock, Boyd and Sanders, holds that God does not exhaustively know or settle the future and genuinely changes His mind as history unfolds; process theology goes further and denies immutability and omnipotence outright. Samuel's title answers both in seven words: the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent, for he is not a man, that he should repent. Balaam is made to say the same thing, Malachi grounds Israel's survival in “I am the LORD, I change not”, and James says every good gift comes from the Father with whom is no variableness nor shadow of turning. A God who deliberates like a man is not the God of Scripture, and no promise of His could be trusted further than His next revision.

A second failure belongs to careless defenders of the doctrine, who meet the chapter's own statement that it repented the LORD that He had set up Saul by emptying the words of all content. Scripture is doing something more careful. God's dealings with men genuinely change as men change — He threatens Nineveh and spares it on repentance — while His nature and eternal purpose do not move at all; the Westminster and Baptist confessions say He is immutable and yet most just and terrible in His judgments. The principle to recover is both halves. Immutability is not divine indifference, and the relenting language is not divine instability; it is the unchangeable God dealing variously with changeable men.
roots_summary: Hebrew netsach, perpetuity or victory (the AV margin glosses both); with shaqar, to lie, and nacham, to relent — both denied of Him because He is not a man.
roots_lines: Hebrew netsach, perpetuity, endurance, pre-eminence; hence strength that lasts.
The AV margin glosses the title ‘or, Eternity, or, Victory’.
Hebrew shaqar, to lie or deal falsely, denied of God in the same verse.
Hebrew nacham, to repent or relent, denied of Him as of a man.
Spoken to Saul after the sparing of Agag, 1 Samuel 15:22-29.
